summary: Describes the NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol. A host or router on a non-broadcast multi-access network, such as ATM, can use it to find the addresses needed to reach the next hop toward a destination, often allowing a direct shortcut.

plainLanguage.summary: NHRP lets a computer on a network that cannot broadcast, such as an ATM network, find out how to reach another computer directly. A server on the network looks up the address and answers with the network address of the best next hop. The sender can then open a direct connection to it instead of routing the traffic through several computers.

questions: how do hosts find shortcuts on atm networks
what is a next hop server
subtitle: How a host or router on a non-broadcast network like ATM asks servers for the address of its next hop, so traffic can take a direct shortcut.

tldr.problem: On a non-broadcast, multi-access network such as ATM, ordinary ARP only works inside one logical IP subnet, so traffic between subnets crosses extra router hops even though the network could carry it directly.
tldr.mechanism: A source sends an NHRP Resolution Request toward the destination along the routed path. The Next Hop Server that serves the destination replies with the NBMA address of the destination, or of the egress router nearest to it.
tldr.outcome: The source can then reach the next hop directly, for example by opening a connection, instead of crossing intermediate routers. Authentication, caching and loop-avoidance rules keep the exchange safe.

today: RFC 2332 is a Proposed Standard published in April 1998. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a functional superset of the NBMA Address Resolution Protocol, and the RFC notes that applying it to broadcast networks is possible but left for further study.

sections.title: Why NHRP Exists
sections.content:
The NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol lets a source station, a host or router that wants to communicate over a Non-Broadcast, Multi-Access subnetwork, determine the internetworking layer addresses and NBMA addresses of suitable NBMA next hops toward a destination station. A subnetwork can be non-broadcast either because it does not support broadcasting, as an X.25 subnetwork does, or because broadcasting is not feasible, as with an SMDS multicast group or an extended Ethernet.

One model of an NBMA network uses logically independent IP subnets, LISs. All members of an LIS share the same IP network number and address mask, are directly connected to the same NBMA subnetwork, reach everything outside the LIS through a router, and reach each other directly without routers. Address resolution as described in the IP addressing documents resolves the next hop address only when the destination is in the same LIS as the source. Otherwise the source must hand the packet to a router that belongs to several LISs. In multi-LIS configurations, hop-by-hop address resolution may not be enough to resolve the NBMA next hop, and IP packets may take several IP hops through the NBMA subnetwork.

The alternative model uses Local Address Groups, where the decision to forward locally or remotely is decoupled from addressing and tied instead to quality of service and traffic characteristics. Supporting that model assumes a mechanism that lets any entity on an NBMA network resolve an internetworking layer address to an NBMA address for any other entity on the same network, whatever the address assignments are. NHRP describes such a mechanism. Once the next hop is resolved, the source may either start sending IP packets straight to the destination, on a connectionless NBMA network such as SMDS, or first establish a connection with the desired bandwidth, on a connection-oriented NBMA network such as ATM.

NHRP is also able to determine the egress point from an NBMA subnetwork when the destination is not directly connected to it and the egress router is not learned by other means such as routing protocols. It is intended to reduce or eliminate the extra router hops required by the LIS model, and it can be deployed without interfering with existing ARP services.
sections.plainLanguage: On some networks, such as ATM, a computer cannot ask everyone on the network who owns an address, the way it can on an ordinary Ethernet. NHRP gives it another way to find out, and it can then cut straight across the network instead of handing the packet to a series of routers.

sections.title: The Roles and the Resolution Flow
sections.content:
A physical NBMA subnetwork may be partitioned for administrative and policy reasons into several disjoint logical NBMA subnetworks, each a collection of hosts and routers that share unfiltered subnetwork connectivity. Within a logical NBMA subnetwork sit one or more entities that implement NHRP. Those capable of answering NHRP Resolution Requests are called Next Hop Servers (NHSs), and they serve sets of destination hosts that may or may not be directly connected to the subnetwork. The stations that send NHRP requests are Next Hop Clients (NHCs). A station that has no NHS functionality of its own is an NHC, and an NHS is said to serve it.

Each NHS keeps a cache of protocol layer address to NBMA subnetwork layer address resolution information, built from NHRP Register packets, from Resolution Requests and Replies, or from mechanisms outside the scope of the RFC such as ARP or preconfigured tables. An NHC keeps a similar cache, filled from Resolution Replies, manual configuration, or outside mechanisms. For a serving NHS to supply information for an NHC, NHSs must exist at each hop along the routed path between the requesting NHC and the destination. Resolution Requests are not forwarded to destination NHCs; they are processed by the serving NHS.

The flow starts when station S wants to resolve the NBMA address of a path to destination D, most likely because a data packet for D is about to be sent. S first finds the next hop to D through normal routing, and uses the cache if the answer is already there. Otherwise, if the next hop is reachable through one of its NBMA interfaces, S builds an NHRP Resolution Request carrying D's internetworking layer address as the target, S's own address as the source, and S's NBMA addressing information. S may also ask for an authoritative reply only. While waiting, S may drop the data packet, hold it until a better path is available, or forward it along the routed path, which is the recommended default. A Resolution Request for a given destination MUST NOT be triggered on every packet.

When the NHS receives the request it checks whether it serves D. If not, it forwards the request to another NHS. If it does serve D, it resolves D's NBMA address and sends back an authoritative Resolution Reply. A transit NHS may cache the information and answer later requests with it, but NHSs MUST NOT respond to authoritative Resolution Requests with cached information. When no NHS can answer, a negative reply (NAK) is returned, either because no binding is known or because an NHS could not forward the request.
sections.plainLanguage: Two roles appear throughout the protocol. The client is the host or router that needs an answer. The server is the router that knows the answers and serves the destination. The client asks along the routed path, the server that serves the destination answers, and any router in between may remember the answer.

sections.title: How an NHRP Packet Is Built
sections.content:
Every NHRP packet has a Fixed Part, a Mandatory Part and an Extensions Part. The Fixed Part is common to all packet types and is fixed at 20 octets. The Mandatory Part MUST be present but varies with the packet type, and its length is determined by the contents of the extensions offset field: if that field is zero the mandatory part runs to the end of the packet, otherwise it ends where the extensions begin. The Extensions Part also varies by packet type and need not be present at all.

The fixed header carries the address family number, which says what kind of link layer addresses are carried; a protocol type field, which is a 16-bit number space where 0x0000 to 0x00FF is for protocols defined by equivalent NLPIDs and 0x0600 to 0xFFFF for protocols defined by equivalent Ethertypes; a protocol SNAP field for the long form of protocol identification; a hop count; the total packet size in octets; the standard IP checksum over the whole packet; the extensions offset; the operation version, where 1 means NHRP as defined in the document; the operation type; and the type and length of the source NBMA address and subaddress.

The hop count gives the maximum number of NHSs a packet may traverse before it is discarded, and is used like a time to live: each NHS decrements it, and an NHS that receives a packet with the count at zero sends an Error Indication back to the source and drops the packet. An error indication is never sent in reply to an error indication. The operation type values are 1 for Resolution Request, 2 for Resolution Reply, 3 for Registration Request, 4 for Registration Reply, 5 for Purge Request, 6 for Purge Reply and 7 for Error Indication. Values from 128 to 255 are reserved for research or other protocol development.

On the wire, NHRP packets are carried at the NBMA layer using the encapsulation of the underlying network. SMDS always uses LLC/SNAP, ATM uses either LLC/SNAP or no encapsulation on connections dedicated to a single protocol, and Frame Relay and X.25 use NLPID/SNAP with a NLPID of 0x0080.
sections.plainLanguage: Every NHRP packet starts with the same 20 bytes of header, which says what kind of addresses it holds, how long the packet is, how many servers it may pass through, and which of the seven message types it is. The rest of the packet holds the addresses themselves, and optional extensions.

sections.title: Resolution Requests and Replies
sections.content:
The mandatory part of the request and reply messages has a common header and zero or more Client Information Entries, or CIEs. A CIE carries a code, a prefix length, the maximum transmission unit for the client, a holding time in seconds, the type and length of the next hop NBMA address and subaddress, the length of the client protocol address, a preference value, and the client's NBMA address, subaddress and protocol address. Higher preference values mean a more preferred entry, and the first CIE in a Resolution Reply MUST contain the next hop with the highest preference so that a minimal client needs to parse only one entry.

The Resolution Request has type code 1 and carries zero or one CIE, which holds information about the client sending the request. Its flags are Q, set when the sender is a router; A, set when only authoritative next hop information is wanted; D, unused; U, the uniqueness bit, set when the client wants a binding that is known to be unique; and S, set when the binding between the source protocol address and the source NBMA information is guaranteed to be stable and accurate. The Destination Protocol Address in the common header holds the address of the station for which resolution is desired, and the request must be sent directly to one of the client's serving NHSs.

The Resolution Reply has type code 2 and holds one or more CIEs matching the request. The A flag in the reply is set when the next hop information is authoritative. An NHS is an authoritative source when the cached information came from a Registration Request or from synchronization with an NHS that obtained it that way. Non-authoritative information is what an NHS picks up by listening to other NHRP packets, and the distinction exists so that a source whose attempt based on non-authoritative information fails can ask again authoritatively.

When no match is found, the reply carries a NAK code instead of a binding. The defined codes are 4 for Administratively Prohibited, 5 for Insufficient Resources, 12 for no internetworking layer address to NBMA address binding existing, 13 for the binding existing but not being unique, and 14 for the unique internetworking layer address already being registered. A reply with a NAK code other than zero MUST NOT contain any other CIE.
sections.plainLanguage: The request asks for one address, and the reply gives one or more candidates in order of preference. Some replies say no: the address is not known, the server is short of resources, or policy forbids the answer. A separate flag lets a client insist on an answer that came from the station that owns the address rather than from a cached copy.

sections.title: Deployment Rules
sections.content:
Resolution Requests travel one or more hops inside an NBMA subnetwork. Each station, including the source, picks a neighbouring NHS to forward the request to, typically by applying the destination protocol layer address to the routing table and using the resulting routing decision. Although a protocol layer address is used to make the routing decision, NHRP packets are not encapsulated in a protocol layer header; they are carried at the NBMA layer.

The NHS serving a destination must lie along the routed path to that destination. In practice this means that all egress routers must double as NHSs for the destinations beyond them, hosts on the subnetwork are served by routers that double as NHSs, and forwarding NHRP packets requires a contiguous deployment of NHRP-capable routers. All NHSs within a LIS or LAG should have at least some part of their resolution databases synchronized, so that a packet arriving at one router is forwarded the same way as a packet arriving at another. One method is the Server Cache Synchronization Protocol, and the RFC recommends it when a LIS or LAG contains two or more router/NHSs.

During a migration to NHRP not every router can be expected to be NHRP capable, so NHRP traffic that would have to cross such a router is expected to be dropped because the packet is not recognized. A client that has tried and failed to acquire a cut-through path should fall back to the network layer routed path. Where the NBMA technology offers a group, anycast or multicast address, a client may be configured with one that is assigned to all NHSs serving its routing realm, to establish an initial connection for a registration request; that address must not be used for sending NHRP requests, and the resulting connection may be used only if the registration response arrives over it.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol only works if the servers are placed so that the request can walk along the route to the destination, one server after another, with no gaps. Where a gap exists, the traffic falls back to the ordinary routed path.

sections.title: Caching Rules
sections.content:
Cache management differs between the three kinds of station. A source station MUST cache all received Resolution Replies it is actively using, and MUST cache incomplete entries, those for which a request was sent but no reply received, in order to preserve the request ID for retries and to avoid sending a request for every data packet. It MUST purge expired information and MUST purge the appropriate entries on receipt of a Purge Request.

A serving NHS SHOULD cache protocol address information from the requests it has answered, where the information in the reply could change during its lifetime, so that a Purge Request can be issued. The internetworking to NBMA binding supplied by the source in a request may be cached only if the S bit is set, the request carried a CIE with a holding time greater than zero, and only for non-authoritative use, for no longer than that holding time.

A transit NHS may cache source binding information from forwarded requests under the same conditions, and may cache destination information from a reply's CIE only if the D bit is set, again for non-authoritative use only and only until the holding time expires. It MUST NOT cache source binding information contained in a Resolution Reply. Cached information must be discarded when the prescribed time has expired, and it may be returned only in response to non-authoritative requests.

The RFC also explains how stale information behaves. For destinations attached directly to the subnetwork the mappings are static, and a stale entry causes a loss of connectivity that may trigger an authoritative request. For destinations off the subnetwork the mapping may be very dynamic, and stale information then leads to a suboptimal path rather than a loss of connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers remember the addresses they have learned so they do not have to look them up again. The rules are strict about what may be kept: an entry may be used to answer ordinary requests, but it may not be passed off as the official answer.

sections.title: Loops, Prefixes and the Domino Effect
sections.content:
Section 6.1 warns that a stable routing loop may occur if NHRP is used between two routers, in particular when a path across a boundary loses information used in route selection, such as the loss of BGP path vector information or the interworking of routing protocols with dissimilar metrics. In such circumstances NHRP should not be used. The situation can be avoided if there are no back door paths between the entry and egress router outside the NBMA subnetwork.

Section 6.3 restricts how the prefix length of a CIE may be used. An NHS that wants to send a prefix must examine the network layer reachability information of the route it would use toward the destination and extract the shortest prefix that covers the destination and is not a superset of any route the NHS holds. The field should be used with restraint, because a too large set of destinations can cause suboptimal routing, and this document specifies its use only when all destinations covered by the prefix are stable, meaning either that they are all on the NBMA network or that they are all directly attached to the responding station.

Section 6.4 describes the NHRP domino effect. If a router forwards a data packet without waiting for an NHRP transit path, the next router along the path may do the same and start its own Resolution Request, so one packet can trigger a request at every router along the path. At best this produces excessive NHRP traffic, and at worst an excessive number of virtual circuits. NHRP implementations for NHSs MUST provide a mechanism to avoid or suppress this behavior, for example by configuring a router so that only traffic received over its non-NBMA interfaces triggers Resolution Requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things can go wrong in practice. The shortcut can send packets in a circle. A shortcut can be offered for a group of addresses when only one of them would work. And one packet can set off a chain of lookups along the whole path. The RFC sets rules for each case.

sections.title: Authentication and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The NHRP Authentication Extension carries authentication information between NHRP speakers and may be included in any NHRP request or reply. Authentication is always done pairwise, hop by hop: the extension is regenerated at each hop. A received packet that fails the authentication test makes the station generate an Error Indication of type Authentication Failure and discard the packet.

The extension carries a Security Parameter Index, which acts as an index into a table of keys and other information such as the hash algorithm, a source address field, and authentication data. The source address is the address assigned to the outgoing interface, and the tuple of SPI and source address identifies the key in use. The authentication data field holds a keyed hash calculated over the entire NHRP payload, with that field zeroed out before the hash is computed. SPIs may be negotiated manually or with an Internet key management protocol, and manual keying MUST be supported. The algorithm identifies the hash agreed by the two entities, with HMAC-MD5-128 as the default and other algorithms allowed by registering new values.

The security considerations state that the keys must be strong and the algorithms correctly implemented, because the security of the whole system depends on it. Security is performed hop by hop, so the data can be trusted only as far as all the entities on the path can be trusted; a chain of trust is established among the NHRP entities along the path, and compromising one of them compromises the whole NHRP domain. Data integrity covers the entire payload, which guarantees that the message was not modified and that the source is authenticated. Without the extension, or where security is compromised, NHRP entities are exposed to spoofing, active and passive attacks. There is no mechanism to encrypt the messages, so a standard layer 3 confidentiality mechanism is assumed to be used.

Any NHS is susceptible to denial of service attacks that overload it. A rogue host can send request and registration packets to the first hop NHS. Without authentication, the registration packet is forwarded along the routed path and processed at each NHS; with authentication, only the first hop NHS is exposed, because unauthenticated packets are dropped rather than forwarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server can add a fingerprint to the packets it sends, so that the next server can check that they really came from the previous one. The fingerprint is checked hop by hop, so a chain of trusted servers gives a chain of trust. The packets themselves are not encrypted, and the RFC says a normal network-level encryption mechanism is expected for that.

fields.name: Address family
fields.desc: Number identifying the kind of link layer addresses carried.

fields.name: Protocol type
fields.desc: Identifies the protocol of the addresses carried.

fields.name: Protocol SNAP
fields.desc: Long form protocol identification; zero unless the protocol type is 0x0080.

fields.name: Hop count
fields.desc: Maximum number of NHSs the packet may traverse.

fields.name: Packet size
fields.desc: Total length of the NHRP packet in octets.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Standard IP checksum over the whole NHRP packet.

fields.name: Extensions offset
fields.desc: Offset of the first extension; zero when there are none.

fields.name: Operation version
fields.desc: 1 means NHRP as defined in this document.

fields.name: Operation type
fields.desc: Which of the seven NHRP message types this is.

fields.name: Source address type and length
fields.desc: Type and length of the source NBMA address.

fields.name: Source subaddress type and length
fields.desc: Type and length of the source NBMA subaddress; zero when there is none.

items.label: Resolution Request
items.desc: Asks for the NBMA address of the next hop toward a destination.

items.label: Resolution Reply
items.desc: Carries the next hop entries, or a NAK code.

items.label: Registration Request
items.desc: Tells an NHS the station's own NBMA information to cache.

items.label: Purge Request
items.desc: Asks that a cached binding be removed.

items.label: Error Indication
items.desc: Reports a problem, such as an exceeded hop count.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC: A RESOLUTION EXCHANGE

messages.label: Resolution Request
messages.note: Carries the destination protocol address to resolve.

messages.label: Registration
messages.note: The destination registers its own NBMA address with the server.

messages.label: Resolution Reply
messages.note: Returns the NBMA address of the next hop.

viz.caption: NAK CODES USED IN RESOLUTION REPLIES

items.title: Code 4
items.text: Administratively prohibited: the server refuses for policy or routing reasons.

items.title: Code 5
items.text: Insufficient resources: the server cannot store what the answer would need.

items.title: Code 12
items.text: No internetworking layer address to NBMA address binding exists.

items.title: Code 13
items.text: The binding exists but is not unique.

items.title: Code 14
items.text: The unique internetworking layer address is already registered.
